name: Q10
seoDesc: Q10: work out temperature (T₁) from the temperature and the reaction rate. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: temperature (T₁) is what the Temperature coefficient (Q==10==) calculator works out, and it gets there from the temperature, the reaction rate and the temperature coefficient. Think of it as a shortcut for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Q10 calculator work?
sections.html:
The Temperature coefficient (Q==10==) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports temperature (T₁) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the temperature (T₂), the reaction rate (R₁) and the temperature coefficient (Q₁₀).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Q10 calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Temperature (T₁)=temperature (T₂) − the natural log of (reaction rate (R₂) ÷ reaction rate (R₁)) ÷ the natural log of (-1 ÷ 4 × the square root of (5) × (temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) ^ 1 ÷ 10) + (1 ÷ 4) × (temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) ^ 1 ÷ 10) + (1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (2) × (temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) ^ 1 ÷ 10) × the square root of (-5 − the square root of (5)))
Temperature (T₁)=temperature (T₂) − 10 × the natural log of (reaction rate (R₂) ÷ reaction rate (R₁)) ÷ the natural log of (temperature coefficient (Q₁₀))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Temperature (T₂) = 10 °C, Reaction rate (R₁) = 10, Reaction rate (R₂) = 10 and Temperature coefficient (Q₁₀) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Temperature (T₁) = 10 °C.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Temperature (T₁) = 10 °C should be roughly the size you expected from Temperature (T₂) = 10 °C and Reaction rate (R₁) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in Celsius, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Temperature coefficient (Q==10==) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the temperature, the reaction rate and the temperature coefficient — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Q10 calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns temperature (T₁), derived from the temperature, the reaction rate and the temperature coefficient. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Q10 calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the temperature, the reaction rate and the temperature coefficient, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature (T₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature (T₁) opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Temperature (T₁) = 10 °C. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Q10 calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
